question: I am expecting to graduate from Mitb in Dec 2026. I have just accepted a job offer with google how much do I need to save to buy a flat nearby for a flat suitable for mitb graduate?
answer:
I can’t tell you how much you personally need to save. That depends on your flat choice, loan type, grant eligibility, and your own finances, which the official sources here do not cover for your case.

In general, the cash/CPF you need depends first on financing. With a bank loan, the minimum downpayment is 25% of the purchase price, and 5% of that must be in cash; OA savings may be used for the rest. With an HDB loan, the minimum downpayment is 20% and it can be fully paid using OA savings. Bank-loan buyers must have a valid Letter of Offer when they exercise the Option to Purchase; HDB-loan buyers must have a valid HFE letter then and when submitting the resale application. MAS/HDB loan rules such as LTV, tenure and minimum cash payment also apply. [5][6][1]

If you take an HDB loan, you must first use your OA savings for the purchase up to the prevailing limits, though each buyer may retain up to $20,000 in OA. CPF use also depends on the flat’s remaining lease, property type and loan type, and CPF can be used for purchase price, housing loan, stamp and legal fees. [1][2][3][4][7]

You may also need upfront cash for the resale Option Fee (up to $1,000) and total deposit (up to $5,000). [6]

Grants may reduce what you need to fund. Families may apply for CPF Housing Grant, EHG, Step-Up Grant and PHG, depending on eligibility. Singles grants can be credited to eligible applicants’ OA and used to offset the purchase price or reduce the housing loan; for the Singles Grant, the income ceiling is $8,000 if buying alone, or $16,000 if buying with family or other singles. [8][9][10][11]

question: I am a foreigner and I just move to Singapore planning to buy a flat at least 1 million, what is the process that I need to do?
answer:
If you are only a foreigner who has just moved to Singapore, I couldn’t confirm from the official HDB sources I have that you can buy an HDB resale flat. The sources say the buyer must be a Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident, at least 21 years old, and must apply with at least one other Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident to form a core family nucleus. A single person buying alone must be a Singapore Citizen aged 35 or above. If any buyer/core family member is an SPR, they must have held SPR status for at least 3 years at the time of the HFE application. [1]

If you do meet those status rules, the process is broadly:
1. Apply for an HDB Flat Eligibility (HFE) letter first. HDB uses this to assess your eligibility to buy and financing options. [1][2]
2. Make sure you have financing in place: enough CPF/cash/loan, and either an HFE letter for an HDB loan or a bank’s Letter of Offer. [2][3]
3. Check the Ethnic Integration Policy and SPR quota at the OTP stage, when exercising the OTP, and again when submitting the resale application. [2]
4. Submit the resale application through the HDB Flat Portal using Singpass. [1][3]

Other key restrictions: you can buy only one flat for owner-occupation, must physically and continuously occupy it, and there is a 5-year minimum occupation period with further restrictions on renting out and buying other residential property. [1]

Please check the latest HDB page before acting, as HDB applies prevailing rules. [1]

question: My brother transferred his HDB flat to me without selling it, but I need to pay for his CPF refund. Can I take an HDB loan? Can I still use the HDB grant given in HFE?
answer:
I could not confirm from the official sources I have that you personally “need to pay” your brother’s CPF refund in every transfer case. What the rules say is: when a flat is transferred other than by sale, the outgoing owner may be required to refund CPF monies to his own CPF account, and the incoming owner may apply to use the incoming owner’s CPF to pay all or part of that refund, subject to CPF Board approval and conditions.[1] If a share is transferred, CPF principal used plus accrued interest must be refunded based on the member’s share, and extra cash may be needed if that member used more CPF than his share.[2]

On the HDB loan: if you need financing to buy or take over ownership of a flat, you may apply for an HDB housing loan or a loan from a financial institution.[4] HDB will grant a housing loan only if you meet its eligibility conditions, and you must also meet HDB’s credit assessment criteria.[4][5] If you do not meet HDB’s eligibility conditions, you must take a loan from a financial institution if you need mortgage financing.[4] A valid HFE letter is required for an HDB housing loan application for a resale flat, and it must still be valid when the resale application is submitted.[4][5]

The passages say an HFE letter states your eligibility to buy a new or resale flat and the amount of grants and HDB loan you are eligible for, but they do not say whether a grant indicated in HFE can be used for a flat transfer instead of a purchase.[4] Please check the latest official HDB guidance for transfer cases.

question: Can I use CPF for a resale flat, and what do 4-room flats in Tampines usually sell for?
answer:
Yes. You can use CPF Ordinary Account savings to buy an HDB resale flat, including for the downpayment, housing loan instalments, stamp fees and legal fees, and Home Protection Scheme premiums where applicable.[3]

Key rules and limits:
- If you take an HDB loan, each buyer may keep up to $20,000 in their OA; the remaining OA balance must be used for the flat purchase before the HDB loan can be granted.[1][4]
- CPF use is subject to limits. The amount you can use depends on whether the flat’s remaining lease can cover the youngest owner using CPF up to age 95. Once the allowed CPF amount is used up, the rest of the purchase price and/or monthly instalments must be paid in cash.[1][4][6]
- For a resale flat with an HDB loan, CPF withdrawal limits also depend on whether you can set aside the Basic Retirement Sum.[5]
- Occupiers listed in the resale application cannot use their CPF savings for the purchase.[2]
- If you later sell the flat or withdraw ownership, the CPF used plus accrued interest must be refunded to your CPF account.[2]
- For downpayment, an HDB loan’s 20% minimum can be fully paid with OA savings, while for a bank loan the 25% minimum downpayment includes 5% cash.[7]

For Tampines 4-room resale flats, in the latest 12 full months from 2025-10 to 2026-09, the median price was $665,000, the mean was $685,674, and prices ranged from $510,000 to $928,000 across 902 deals.[price]

question: Since singles can't buy resale flats, what's the cheapest 2-room in Yishun?
answer:
That premise is not correct. A single person can buy an HDB resale flat if they are a Singapore citizen who is unmarried, widowed or divorced, and aged 35 and above [1].

For singles buying on their own, HDB says you should apply for an HFE letter first, which will show your eligibility to buy a new or resale flat, and any grants or HDB loan you may qualify for [1]. HDB also specifically contemplates singles buying resale flats on their own under the Singles Grant rules, including for 2- to 4-room resale flats [2].

For property ownership conditions, if you are buying a non-subsidised resale unclassified or Standard flat, and you own private residential property when you apply for the HFE letter, you must dispose of that interest within 6 months of completing the flat purchase [1]. There are also limits on non-residential property ownership [1].

I couldn't find an official passage here that states a separate eligibility rule specific to a 2-room resale flat beyond the singles/resale rules above.

On prices: in Yishun, for 2-room flats, the lowest recorded resale price in the available data from 2017-01 to 2026-10 was $190,000, based on 392 deals.
